item.title: Development and validation of the electrosacrogram (ESG): a digital point-of-care tool for real-time neuro-sacral assessment after spinal cord injury
item.category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients
item.description:
Authors: Maude Duguay; Jean-Marc Mac-Thiong; Juan-David Cifuentes-Hernandez; Natan Bensoussan; Andréane Richard-Denis

Category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients | TRL: 4

Summary: The paper introduces the **ElectroSacroGram (ESG)**, a bedside digital surface-EMG system and protocol that quantitatively measures sacral motor, reflex, and sensory function in real time after spinal cord or cauda equina injury, providing objective metrics that strongly agree with expert digital rectal examination while achieving high diagnostic accuracy against imaging-confirmed lesions. For biorobotics, ESG supplies a standardized, EMG-based neural readout of sacral circuitry that can be leveraged for **closed-loop neuromodulation, decoder calibration, and longitudinal monitoring** of neuro-sacral function, enabling more precise control and evaluation of neuroprosthetic and rehabilitation robots targeting pelvic, bladder, and lower-limb function.

DOI: 10.1186/s12984-025-01797-4

item.title: Surface electromyography vs clinical outcome measures after robot-assisted gait training in patients with spinal cord injury after post-acute phase of rehabilitation
item.category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients
item.description:
Authors: Bogumił Korczyński; Justyna Frasuńska; Anna Poświata; Anna Siemianowicz; Michał Mikulski; Beata Tarnacka

Category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients | TRL: 5

Summary: The paper demonstrates that **surface EMG (sEMG) can sensitively capture training‑induced changes in lower-limb muscle activation during Lokomat robot-assisted gait training in sub‑acute incomplete SCI**, and relates these changes to standard clinical outcome measures in 64 patients. By quantitatively decoding muscle activation patterns rather than relying solely on functional scores, the work highlights sEMG as a **biomarker and control-relevant signal** that could inform adaptive control, patient-specific tuning, and objective performance monitoring in rehabilitation robots, advancing closed‑loop and biomimetic strategies in biorobotics.

DOI: 10.26444/aaem/189609

item.title: Neural correlates of kinematic features of passive finger movement revealed by univariate and multivariate fMRI analyses
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Gustavo S. P. Pamplona; James Sulzer; Ewa Beldzik; Olivier Lambercy; Silvio Ionta; Roger Gassert; Jarrod Lewis-Peacock

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 5

Summary: The paper uses fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis during **robot-controlled passive finger joint movements** to show that human sensorimotor areas encode detailed kinematic features (e.g., joint angle, velocity) even in the absence of active motor commands. By mapping how specific kinematic parameters are represented across primary sensorimotor and associated regions, it provides a quantitative neural “encoding model” of passive hand mechanics that can inform biorobotic hand design and control, particularly for prosthetics and rehabilitation robots that rely on decoding or stimulating proprioceptive-like signals.

Summary: The paper introduces an **AI-integrated EMG-driven hand exoskeleton** that uses surface EMG and a learning-based intention detection framework to decode user-specific finger flexion/extension intentions in real time and drive a multi-DOF rehabilitation robot accordingly. By tightly coupling EMG pattern recognition with low-latency hand actuation, the system enables more intuitive, volitional control for stroke survivors, highlighting a scalable **human–robot interface** architecture that can inform next-generation biorobotic designs for fine hand function restoration.

item.title: Properties of the surface electromyogram following traumatic spinal cord injury: a scoping review
item.category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients
item.description:
Authors: Gustavo Balbinot; Guijin Li; Matheus Joner Wiest; Maureen Pakosh; Julio Cesar Furlan; Sukhvinder Kalsi-Ryan; Jose Zariffa

Category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients | TRL: 2

Summary: The paper systematically characterizes how **surface EMG (sEMG) signal properties change after traumatic spinal cord injury**, showing consistent alterations in amplitude, timing, spectral content, and motor unit behavior that reflect residual but re-organized spinal motor commands. Its key innovation is to reinterpret these altered sEMG features as **informative biomarkers of residual motor command and neuromuscular integrity**, providing a structured framework for decoding motor intent in “clinically complete” SCI where conventional assessments see no function. For biorobotics, this positions multi‑channel and high‑density sEMG as a rich control and feedback modality for neuroprostheses and exoskeletons, enabling more sensitive motor decoding, adaptive controllers, and personalized rehabilitation strategies that exploit subtle residual descending drive rather than relying solely on overt voluntary movement.

DOI: 10.1186/s12984-021-00888-2

item.title: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation: neuromodulation of the suprascapular nerve and brachial plexus for postoperative analgesia following ambulatory rotator cuff repair. A proof-of-concept study
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Brian M Ilfeld; John J Finneran; Rodney A Gabriel; Engy T Said; Patrick L Nguyen; Wendy B Abramson; Bahareh Khatibi; Jacklynn F Sztain; Matthew W Swisher; Pia Jaeger; Dana C Covey; Matthew J Meunier; Eric R Hentzen; Catherine M Robertson

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 7

Summary: This proof-of-concept study demonstrates **ultrasound-guided percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS)** of the suprascapular nerve and brachial plexus using small, temporary, implantable leads to provide postoperative analgesia after ambulatory rotator cuff repair, avoiding continuous local anesthetic infusions. The key innovation is minimally invasive, *preoperative* ultrasound-guided lead placement enabling targeted neuromodulation of proximal shoulder nerves with an external stimulator, suggesting a scalable, modular interface concept that could inform **biorobotic systems for closed-loop motor–sensory neuromodulation**, peripherally implanted sensor–actuator networks, and non-opioid, wearable neuroprosthetic pain-control strategies.

item.title: State-based decoding of hand and finger kinematics using neuronal ensemble and LFP activity during dexterous reach-to-grasp movements
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Vikram Aggarwal; Mohsen Mollazadeh; Adam G. Davidson; Marc H. Schieber; Nitish V. Thakor

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces a **two-stage, state-based decoding framework** in which local field potential (LFP) features from motor cortex first classify behavioral epochs (baseline, reaction, movement, hold), and this LFP-based state decoder then *triggers* a spike-based Kalman filter to continuously decode 3D hand position plus 18 wrist and finger joint angles during reach-to-grasp movements. By optimally combining LFPs for autonomous state switching with spikes for high-fidelity kinematics, the approach significantly improves decoding accuracy over spike-only decoders and provides a more robust, behavior-aware control strategy. For biorobotics, this architecture offers a practical way to achieve **stable, multi-DOF neuroprosthetic and robotic hand control**, minimizing unintended movements during posture while enhancing fine finger and grasp kinematics during active movement.

DOI: 10.1152/jn.01038.2011

PDF: Open Access PDF

item.title: Decoding and geometry of ten finger movements in human posterior parietal cortex and motor cortex
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Charles Guan; Tyson Aflalo; Kelly Kadlec; Jorge Gámez de Leon; Emily R Rosario; Ausaf Bari; Nader Pouratian; Richard A Andersen

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 6

Summary: This study demonstrates the first decoding of individual movements for all **ten fingers** (contralateral and ipsilateral) from human **posterior parietal cortex (PPC)** using 96-channel intracortical arrays in tetraplegic participants, with a factorized neural code separating finger type from laterality and similar representational geometry across hand pairs. PPC signals enabled online brain-machine interface (BMI) control of prosthetic fingers surpassing prior finger BMIs, complemented by motor cortex (MC) recordings showing analogous tuning. For **biorobotics**, this innovation advances intuitive, high-resolution neural prosthetics for hand restoration in paralysis, enabling dexterous multi-finger control via stable PPC representations.

DOI: 10.1088/1741-2552/acd3b1

item.title: Neurorobotic fusion of prosthetic touch, kinesthesia, and movement in bionic upper limbs promotes intrinsic brain behaviors
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Paul D. Marasco; Jacqueline S. Hebert; Jonathon W. Sensinger; Dylan T. Beckler; Zachary C. Thumser; Ahmed W. Shehata; Heather E. Williams; Kathleen R. Wilson

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 7

Summary: The paper introduces a **neurorobotic fusion** of **targeted sensory reinnervation (TSR)** for touch and kinesthesia with **targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR)** for intuitive motor control in a closed-loop neural-machine interface for bionic upper-limb prostheses. In two proximal arm amputees, this integration restored near-able-bodied performance in tasks like grasp force control, stiffness discrimination (e.g., 68-83% accuracy), error correction, and natural visuomotor behaviors, outperforming standard prostheses. For **biorobotics research**, it demonstrates that multimodal sensory-motor restoration enables human-like decision-making and function, establishing a framework for advancing bidirectional neural interfaces.

DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.abf3368

item.title: Decoding hand kinematics from population responses in sensorimotor cortex during grasping
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Elizaveta V Okorokova; James M Goodman; Nicholas G Hatsopoulos; Sliman J Bensmaia

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces a key innovation in intracortical decoding by accurately estimating kinematics across **30 hand joints** (angles outperforming velocities) from small populations of neurons in sensorimotor cortex and superior colliculus (SC), enabling precise control of dexterous hand movements in brain-machine interfaces (BMIs). Unlike prior proximal limb decoders, it leverages SC's postural representations, which could be exploited via intracortical stimulation to close the sensorimotor loop. For biorobotics, this advances high-fidelity neural control of multi-jointed prosthetic hands, potentially transforming rehabilitation by restoring naturalistic manipulation beyond reach-and-grasp paradigms.

DOI: 10.1088/1741-2552/ab95ea

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 6

Summary: This study introduces an **EMG-driven hand exoskeleton** (Hand of Hope) that uses **myoelectric pattern recognition** to detect and interpret motion intent from forearm EMG signals in chronic stroke patients with no voluntary finger movement, enabling real-time assistance for six hand motions (e.g., whole hand close/open, tripod pinch, "gun" sign). item.title: Decoding Handwriting Trajectories from Intracortical Brain Signals for Brain‐to‐Text Communication
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Guangxiang Xu; Zebin Wang; Kedi Xu; Junming Zhu; Jianmin Zhang; Yueming Wang; Yaoyao Hao

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces an innovative decoding framework using an **LSTM-based model** with shape and temporal distortion compensation to reconstruct highly accurate, human-recognizable handwriting trajectories (correlation coefficient >0.75) from intracortical signals recorded via Utah arrays in the motor cortex of a paralyzed patient during attempted handwriting of complex characters. The framework resolves neural-movement misalignment via dynamic time warping for brain-to-text translation, achieving up to **91.1% recognition rate** on a 1000-character database and enabling multi-day data fusion for sustained performance across languages. For **biorobotics research**, it advances neural prosthetics by demonstrating multidimensional handwriting encoding (including 3D velocity, grip strength, and EMG), paving the way for universal, high-fidelity brain-controlled robotic writing interfaces.

DOI: 10.1002/advs.202505492

item.title: Sensing and decoding the neural drive to paralyzed muscles during attempted movements of a person with tetraplegia using a sleeve array
item.category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients
item.description:
Authors: Jordyn E. Ting; Alessandro Del Vecchio; Devapratim Sarma; Nikhil Verma; Samuel C. Colachis; Nicholas V. Annetta; Jennifer L. Collinger; Dario Farina; Douglas J. Weber

Category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients | TRL: 4

Summary: The key innovation of this study is the development of a **wearable myoelectric sensor array**—a sleeve with 150 embedded electrodes—that enables high-resolution recording and real-time decoding of **motor unit firing rates** from paralyzed muscles in a person with tetraplegia during attempted movements. This approach provides the first direct, noninvasive interface with spinal motor neuron output below the level of spinal cord injury, revealing task-specific neural drive even in the absence of visible movement and enabling accurate decoding of motor intention for potential control of assistive or biorobotic devices. This technology represents a significant advance for biorobotics by offering a practical method to sense and interpret residual neural commands, paving the way for intuitive and responsive neuroprosthetic control in individuals with severe paralysis.

DOI: 10.1152/jn.00220.2021

item.title: AI-driven hybrid rehabilitation: synergizing robotics and electrical stimulation for upper-limb recovery after stroke
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Ismail Ben Abdallah; Yassine Bouteraa; Ahmed Alotaibi

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 4

Summary: This paper introduces an **AI-enhanced hybrid rehabilitation system** integrating a dual-arm robotic platform with **EMG-guided neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES)**, featuring a **Support Vector Machine (SVM)** model for real-time muscle fatigue detection via EMG time-frequency features, enabling adaptive stimulation adjustments in a ROS2-based closed-loop architecture for bilateral upper-limb therapy in stroke survivors. The key innovation lies in its fatigue-aware, personalized control that synergizes robotic assistance with NMES to promote voluntary motor relearning, outperforming traditional open-loop systems, with preliminary trials in three patients showing **44% increased range of motion**, **45% enhanced active torque**, and **95% SVM accuracy**. For **biorobotics research**, it advances intelligent hybrid paradigms by demonstrating measurable neuroplasticity gains and scalability potential through clinician-supervised remote adaptation.

DOI: 10.3389/fbioe.2025.1619247

item.description:
Authors: Charles M. Greenspon; Giacomo Valle; Natalya D. Shelchkova; Taylor G. Hobbs; Ceci Verbaarschot; Thierri Callier; Ev I. Berger-Wolf; Elizaveta V. Okorokova; Brianna C. Miller; Nicholas G. Hatsopoulos; Robert A. Gaunt; Sliman J. Bensmaia

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 4

Summary: This study demonstrates that **multi-electrode intracortical microstimulation (ICMS)** in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) of tetraplegic humans evokes stable, somatotopically matched perceptual fields (PFs) with controllable size, shape, and intensity via amplitude and frequency modulation, where overlapping PFs summate to produce more focal, localizable, and gradated sensations mimicking natural touch. A key innovation is the precise mapping of bionic hand force sensors to corresponding S1 electrodes, enabling amplitude-modulated ICMS to convey object contact force and location with improved dynamic range and discriminability over single-electrode stimulation. For **biorobotics research**, this advances brain-computer interfaces by restoring intuitive tactile feedback for prosthetic control, potentially enhancing grip precision and object manipulation in real-world tasks despite limitations in high-force dynamic range.

item.title: A closed-loop hand prosthesis with simultaneous intraneural tactile and position feedback
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control

Authors: Edoardo D’Anna; Giacomo Valle; Alberto Mazzoni; Ivo Strauss; Francesco Iberite; Jérémy Patton; Francesco M. Petrini; Stanisa Raspopovic; Giuseppe Granata; Riccardo Di Iorio; Marco Controzzi; Christian Cipriani; Thomas Stieglitz; Paolo M. Rossini; Silvestro Micera

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 5

Summary: This paper introduces a **closed-loop hand prosthesis** for transradial amputees that simultaneously delivers **somatotopic intraneural tactile feedback** via implanted electrodes and **proprioceptive position feedback** through sensory substitution, enabling real-time joint angle reproduction (median 9.1° precision) and object discrimination (75.5% accuracy) comparable to healthy individuals. In trials with two amputees, this multimodal approach reduced reliance on visual cues, improved task performance without vision, and supported discrimination of object size and compliance. For **biorobotics research**, it advances bidirectional neural interfaces by demonstrating scalable, efficient integration of rich sensory cues, paving the way for sophisticated bionic limbs with enhanced embodiment and functionality.

item.title: Soft robotics and functional electrical stimulation advances for restoring hand function in people with SCI: a narrative review, clinical guidelines and future directions

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 5

Summary: The paper reviews advances in **soft robotics** and **functional electrical stimulation (FES)** wearable devices for restoring hand function in individuals with spinal cord injury, highlighting their promise for both assistive and therapeutic applications. The key innovation is the integration of soft, compliant robotic systems and neuromodulatory FES technologies into portable, user-friendly devices that can detect user intent and facilitate home-based rehabilitation, though challenges remain in standardizing functional assessments and improving device usability for clinical translation. This work underscores the potential impact for biorobotics research by guiding the development of next-generation wearable neurorehabilitation devices that combine mechanical assistance with targeted neuromodulation for personalized motor recovery.

item.description:
Authors: Rinku Roy; Derek G. Kamper; Xiaogang Hu

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 3

Summary: The paper introduces a **neural decoding approach that enables the concurrent prediction of both finger kinematic (movement) and kinetic (force) variables from motor unit discharge patterns**. The key innovation lies in leveraging motor unit activity to simultaneously decode multiple aspects of finger function, which could significantly enhance the control of neural interfaces for biorobotics and prosthetic devices by enabling more natural and precise hand movements. This advancement holds potential to improve dexterous manipulation in robotic hands and next-generation prosthetic systems by providing richer, multi-dimensional control signals derived directly from neural activity.

item.title: Biomimetic sensory feedback through peripheral nerve stimulation improves dexterous use of a bionic hand
item.category: General Biorobotics
item.description:
Authors: J. A. George; D. T. Kluger; T. S. Davis; S. M. Wendelken; E. V. Okorokova; Q. He; C. C. Duncan; D. T. Hutchinson; Z. C. Thumser; D. T. Beckler; P. D. Marasco; S. J. Bensmaia; G. A. Clark

Category: General Biorobotics | TRL: 6

Summary: The paper demonstrates that **biomimetic sensory feedback delivered via peripheral nerve stimulation enables more dexterous and intuitive control of a bionic hand**. The key innovation is a closed-loop system where naturalistic sensory signals, mimicking the temporal and spatial patterns of real touch, are encoded and delivered to the user’s nerves, significantly improving grip precision, object discrimination, and manipulation of fragile items compared to non-biomimetic feedback. This approach marks a major advance for biorobotics by showing that replicating the nervous system’s natural language in artificial limbs can restore both functional and perceptual aspects of touch, paving the way for more lifelike and effective prosthetic devices.

DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.aax2352

item.title: Selectivity and Longevity of Peripheral-Nerve and Machine Interfaces: A Review
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Usman Ghafoor; Sohee Kim; Keum-Shik Hong

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 3

Summary: The paper reviews the **challenges and advancements in peripheral nerve interfaces (PNIs)** for neural prosthetics, emphasizing the need for both **high selectivity** (precise targeting of specific nerve fibers) and **long-term stability** (interface longevity) to achieve effective, naturalistic bidirectional nerve-machine communication. The key innovation discussed is a **hybrid interface approach** that combines the strengths of existing PNI designs to enhance both selectivity and durability, which is critical for reliable sensory feedback and intuitive control in biorobotics applications. This work has significant potential impact for biorobotics research by guiding the development of next-generation neuroprosthetic devices capable of more natural and robust human-machine integration.

item.title: Convolutional neural networks decode finger movements in motor sequence learning from MEG data
item.category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics
item.description:
Authors: Aleksey Zabolotniy; Russell Weili Chan; Victoria Moiseeva; Tommaso Fedele

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: The paper introduces a **compact, physiologically interpretable convolutional neural network (LF-CNN)** that decodes individual finger movements from non-invasive MEG data during motor learning tasks, achieving high accuracy (80–85% for finger identification) with low computational cost and interpretable spatial and spectral features. The key innovation is the LF-CNN’s ability to reliably distinguish overlapping finger representations in the motor cortex, outperforming or matching more complex deep learning models while providing rapid and transparent decoding. This approach enables precise, real-time monitoring of motor learning dynamics, offering significant potential for **biorobotics**—particularly in the development of neuroadaptive prosthetics and closed-loop neurorehabilitation systems that require interpretable, low-latency neural decoding.

By integrating rich multimodal feedback (visual, tactile, and kinesthetic) and serious gaming, the protocol aims to retrain central nervous system circuits and enhance motivation, with potential impact for biorobotics research in designing individualized assistive technologies and advancing understanding of neuroplasticity mechanisms in SCI rehabilitation.

item.title: A Pilot Study of AI-Controlled Transcutaneous Peripheral Nerve Stimulation for Essential Tremor
item.category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control
item.description:
Authors: Richard Dewey; Stuart Isaacson; Richard Dewey; Sagari Betté; Kelly E. Lyons; Zhi Yang; Anh Tuan Nguyen; Qi Zhao; Zhen Zhang; Rajesh Pahwa

Category: Stimulating Peripheral Nerve to Enable Hand And/or Finger Control | TRL: 5

Summary: The key innovation of this pilot study is the development of a **cloud-based, AI-controlled transcutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation (TPNS) device** that delivers personalized, context-dependent stimulation to the radial, median, and ulnar nerves for continuous, all-day management of essential tremor. Unlike traditional patterned stimulation devices, this system uses artificial intelligence to dynamically adjust stimulation parameters in real time based on patient activity and predictive analytics, resulting in significant improvements in tremor severity and daily functioning with minimal side effects. For biorobotics research, this work demonstrates the feasibility and clinical benefit of **integrating adaptive AI algorithms with wearable neuromodulation hardware** to provide closed-loop, individualized therapy, highlighting a promising direction for intelligent, user-responsive assistive devices in neurorehabilitation and movement disorder management.

Summary: The paper introduces **novel complexity measures based on entropy and neural network analysis for electromyography (EMG) signals**, specifically targeting the classification of spinal cord injury (SCI) patients. By quantifying EMG signal complexity, the approach enables more accurate discrimination between healthy and SCI-affected muscle activity, offering a promising tool for adaptive control and patient-specific feedback in **biorobotics and neuroprosthetic systems**. Authors: Z T Irwin; K E Schroeder; P P Vu; A J Bullard; D M Tat; C S Nu; A Vaskov; S R Nason; D E Thompson; J N Bentley; P G Patil; C A Chestek

Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 6

Summary: This study demonstrates the first brain control of fine, **finger-level kinematics** in rhesus macaques by decoding intracortical spikes to continuously control a virtual fingertip using a **Kalman filter**, achieving offline position correlation ρ≈0.78 and real-time target acquisition ≈83% with **~1.01 bits/s information throughput**. The key innovation is a behavioral paradigm for precise virtual fingertip targeting paired with standard spike-based decoding to realize continuous single-finger aperture control, moving BMIs beyond whole-arm control to dexterous hand function. For biorobotics, this establishes a practical pathway to integrate intracortical decoding for **dexterous hand prostheses**, quantifies achievable **throughput** at the finger level comparable to cursor BMIs, and provides a validated task/decoder framework to benchmark next-generation, multi-finger prosthetic controllers and sensory-feedback systems.

item.title: Multimodal decoding and congruent sensory information enhance reaching performance in subjects with cervical spinal cord injury

item.description:

Category: EMG Decoding on Spinal Cord Injured Patients | TRL: 4

Summary: The key innovation of this paper is the development and evaluation of a **multimodal decoding approach** that combines shoulder electromyography (EMG) and gaze tracking to control robot-assisted reaching in individuals with cervical spinal cord injury, demonstrating that integrating disparate physiological signals significantly enhances reach accuracy, especially in highly impaired subjects. The study also shows that **congruent sensory feedback** (proprioceptive input from moving one's own limb) further improves performance when gaze information is unavailable, highlighting the importance of sensory integration for effective neuroprosthetic control. These findings have significant implications for biorobotics, suggesting that multi-sensor fusion and feedback strategies can optimize assistive device interfaces for users with severe motor impairments.

Summary: The paper introduces a **self-folding graphene thin-film cuff electrode** that uses patterned holes and slits in a parylene-based stack to program folding direction, enabling the film to autonomously wrap around peripheral nerves while reducing electrode–electrolyte impedance via slit-mediated ionic access. In vivo on rat sciatic nerve, the cuff reliably wrapped and evoked leg movement with 1 Hz stimulation, and ~80% of devices folded in the intended direction, highlighting a minimally invasive route to interface with finer nerve fibers. For biorobotics, this design offers a lightweight, conformal, and scalable nerve interface leveraging **2D graphene** conductivity and low-impedance access for stable stimulation, potentially improving closed-loop motor control and selective neuromodulation in soft robotic systems.

Summary: The key innovation of this paper is the **integration of spinal motoneuron neural decoding with postural synergy-based soft robotic hand design**, enabling prosthetic hands to achieve natural, multidigit control by mapping neural commands directly to coordinated hand postures. This approach allows users—including prosthesis users—to perform dexterous tasks and in-hand manipulation with high accuracy and intuitiveness, surpassing traditional muscle synergy methods in both robustness and dimensionality. The work represents a significant advance for biorobotics, as it demonstrates a co-design paradigm for prosthetic devices and neural interfaces that closely mimic the sensorimotor integration of natural limbs, potentially transforming human–machine interfacing in rehabilitation and augmentation contexts.

For biorobotics, this establishes a scalable myoelectric decoding pathway for dexterous avatar/robotic arm control and a platform to integrate with neuroprosthetics and closed-loop assistive systems that leverage residual spinal circuitry.

Summary: The key innovation of this paper is a **flexible intracortical brain-computer interface (BCI) that enables high-performance typing by decoding attempted finger flexion/extension movements using neural network velocity decoding, supporting both continuous "point-and-click" and rapid "keystroke" paradigms**. This approach allows users with paralysis to type at speeds up to 90 characters per minute with over 90% accuracy, matching state-of-the-art BCI performance and offering customizable, multi-finger, and bimanual control. Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: The key innovation of this paper is the demonstration that multi-finger movements in the human motor cortex are represented by a "pseudo-linear summation" of the neural activity patterns corresponding to individual finger movements, with normalization mechanisms preventing simple additive scaling as more fingers are involved. This compositional coding principle explains the neural geometry underlying complex finger actions and reveals why non-linear decoding methods outperform linear ones for intracortical brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). The findings have significant implications for biorobotics, as they provide a principled framework for designing more accurate neural decoders for dexterous multi-finger control in robotic prostheses and advanced BCIs.

Summary: The paper introduces a **biomimetic neurostimulation framework** that encodes touch by driving peripheral nerves with time‑variant patterns derived from an in‑silico mechanoreceptor model, yielding spatiotemporal neural activity that closely matches natural touch and propagates to dorsal root ganglia and spinal cord in cats. Category: Intracortical Decoding on Hand and Finger Kinematics | TRL: 4

Summary: The paper demonstrates that while offline decoding of finger kinematics and muscle activity from intracortical recordings in nonhuman primates is significantly degraded by changes in task context (such as altered hand posture or resistance), online brain–machine interface (BMI) control remains robust because the neural manifolds underlying finger movements stay aligned across contexts. The key innovation is the identification that neural population dynamics shift systematically with context, but this shift can be compensated for during real-time BMI use, highlighting the potential for more adaptable and context-robust neural decoders in biorobotics and neuroprosthetic applications. This insight advances the design of BMIs for dexterous hand control in real-world, variable environments.
